```{r}
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
library(htmltools)
source('../../shared-code/plotting.R')
theme_set(blank.theme)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args=list(bg="transparent"))
```

```{r}
curves = list(step     = function(x) { 1*(x >= 0) },
                   line     = function(x) { x },
                   stepline = function(x) { x*(x >= 0) }, 
                   sin      = function(x) { sin(pi*x) })

fourier.series = function(const, sin.coef, cos.coef) {
  k = 1:(length(sin.coef))
  function(x) { 
    as.vector(const + 2 * sin.coef %*% sin(pi*outer(k,x)/2) + 
                      2 * cos.coef %*% cos(pi*outer(k,x))/2)
  }
}

compressed.curve = function(K) {
  k=1:K
   list(step      = fourier.series(1/2, 1/(pi*k), 0*k),
        line      = fourier.series(0,   2*(-1)^(k+1) / (pi*k),   0*k),
        stepline  = fourier.series(1/4, (-1)^(k+1) / (pi*k), ((-1)^k-1)/(pi^2*k^2)),
        sin       = fourier.series(0, .5*(k==2), 0*k))  
}

n=10
X = seq(-1,1,length.out=n)
densepoints = data.frame(X=seq(-1,1,by=.001))

K = 10
compressed.curves = compressed.curve(K)
sigmas = map2(compressed.curves, curves, function(mu.compressed, mu) {
     sd(mu.compressed(X) - mu(X)) 
})

formulas =  list(poly9=Y~poly(X,9), tenpiece.constant=Y~cut(X,10), fivepiece.linear=Y~cut(X,5)*X, 
                 poly3=Y~poly(X,3), fourpiece.constant=Y~cut(X,4), twopiece.linear=Y~cut(X,2)*X,
                 constant=Y~1)
```


```{r}
X = seq(-1,1,length.out=10)
plots = function(X, sigmas, formulas, point.alpha=1) {

n=length(X)
set.seed(1)
Z = sqrt(3)*runif(n, min=-1, max=1)

observations = pmap_dfr(list(curves, compressed.curves, sigmas, names(curves)), function(mu, mu.compressed, sigma, curve) {
    data.frame(X=X, Y.noiseless=mu(X), Y.compressed=mu.compressed(X), Y.random=mu(X)+sigma*Z, curve=curve)
})

fits = pmap_dfr(list(curves, compressed.curves, sigmas, names(curves)), function(mu, mu.compressed, sigma, curve) {
  map_dfr(formulas, .id="formula", function(formula) {  
    noiseless.observations = data.frame(X=X, Y=mu(X))
    compressed.observations = data.frame(X=X, Y=mu.compressed(X))
    random.observations = data.frame(X=X, Y=mu(X)+sigma*Z)
    
    noiseless.model  = lm(formula, data=noiseless.observations)
    random.model     = lm(formula, data=random.observations)
    compressed.model = lm(formula, data=compressed.observations)
    
    densepoints$mu.hat.noiseless  = predict(noiseless.model,  newdata=densepoints)
    densepoints$mu.hat.compressed = predict(compressed.model, newdata=densepoints)
    densepoints$mu.hat.random     = predict(random.model,     newdata=densepoints)
    densepoints$mu     = mu(densepoints$X)
    densepoints$curve = curve
    densepoints
  })
})

plot.curve = function(curve, formula) {
  obs = observations[observations$curve==curve, ]
  fit = fits[fits$curve == curve & fits$formula == formula, ] 
  lims = range(fits[fits$curve == curve, ]$mu.hat.noiseless)
  ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=X, y=Y.noiseless),       data=obs, alpha=point.alpha) +
             geom_line(aes(x=X,  y=mu),                data=fit,  size=1,       alpha=.3) +
             geom_line(aes(x=X,  y=mu.hat.noiseless),  data=fit,  color='blue', alpha=1) +
             ylim(lims[1], lims[2])
}

plot.compressed = function(curve, formula, noiseless.alpha=.5) {
  obs = observations[observations$curve==curve, ]
  fit = fits[fits$curve == curve & fits$formula == formula, ] 
  lims = range(c(fits[fits$curve == curve, ]$mu.hat.compressed, obs$Y.compressed)) 
  ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=X, y=Y.compressed),       data=obs, alpha=point.alpha) +
             geom_line(aes(x=X,  y=mu),                 data=fit,  size=1,       alpha=.3) +
             geom_line(aes(x=X,  y=mu.hat.noiseless),   data=fit,  color='blue', alpha=noiseless.alpha) +
             geom_line(aes(x=X,  y=mu.hat.compressed),  data=fit,  color='red',  alpha=1) + 
             ylim(lims[1], lims[2])
}

plot.random = function(curve, formula, include.compressed=FALSE, noiseless.alpha=.5, compressed.alpha=.7) {
  obs = observations[observations$curve==curve, ]
  fit = fits[fits$curve == curve & fits$formula == formula, ] 
  lims = range(c(fits[fits$curve == curve, ]$mu.hat.random, obs$Y.random))
  p = ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=X, y=Y.random),       data=obs, alpha=point.alpha) +
             geom_line(aes(x=X,  y=mu),                 data=fit,  size=1,         alpha=.3) +
             geom_line(aes(x=X,  y=mu.hat.noiseless),   data=fit,  color='blue',   alpha=noiseless.alpha) +
             geom_line(aes(x=X,  y=mu.hat.random),      data=fit,  color='purple', alpha=1) 
  if(include.compressed) { 
    p + geom_line(aes(x=X,  y=mu.hat.compressed),  data=fit,  color='red',    alpha=compressed.alpha) 
  } else { p  } + ylim(lims[1], lims[2])
}


list(random=plot.random, compressed=plot.compressed, curve=plot.curve)
}

plot = plots(X, sigmas, formulas)
```

## There are good and bad ways to fit the data.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 4
#| layout-nrow: 3
#| layout-valign: bottom
#| fig.width: 3.8
#| fig.asp: .6
 
for(formula in c('poly9', 'tenpiece.constant', 'fivepiece.linear')) {
  for(curve in names(curves)) {
    print(plot$curve(curve, formula))
  }
}
```
-   Even when you fit it perfectly, i.e. interpolate the observations.
-   Even when you see points right on the curve you want to estimate.

## We fit 10 observations with 10-dimensional models. 

This let us fit the observations we had perfectly.
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| layout-nrow: 2
#| layout-valign: bottom
#| fig.width: 3
#| fig.asp: .5

two.curves = c('step', 'line') 
for(curve in names(curves[two.curves])) {
  for(formula in c('poly9', 'tenpiece.constant', 'fivepiece.linear')) {
    print(plot$curve(curve, formula))
  }
}
```


:::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="0"}
What we got between them depended on the model.

-   High-order polynomial fits wiggle.
-   Piecewise-constant fits staircase.
-   Piecewise-linear fits kink.
:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible data-fragment-index="0"}
-   Wiggling can be very bad in places. 
-   Staircasing causes smaller problems.
-   Kinking is somewhere in between.

In essence, higher-order the polynomials $\implies$ bigger problems.
:::

::::

## This matters more if you observe the curve with error

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| layout-nrow: 2
#| layout-valign: bottom
#| fig.width: 4
#| fig.asp: .67

for(curve in names(curves[two.curves])) {
  for(formula in c('poly9', 'tenpiece.constant', 'fivepiece.linear')) {
    print(plot$compressed(curve, formula))
  }
}
```
Even if the errors are pretty small, like these compression errors.

## But less so when you use smaller models

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| layout-nrow: 2
#| layout-valign: bottom
#| fig.width: 4
#| fig.asp: .67

for(curve in names(curves[two.curves])) {
  for(formula in c('poly3', 'fourpiece.constant', 'twopiece.linear')) {
     print(plot$compressed(curve, formula))
  }
}
```
These ones are four parameter models.

## That's still pretty big 
-   One rule of thumb is that you want ten observations per parameter.
    +   That only justifies fitting a constant to the ten we have.
    +   But we've been able to do very well with these larger models.
    +   Especially in the zero-errors case.
-   That rule of thumb assumes errors are of **typical size**.
    +   Our errors here have been zero or very small.
    +   That's what allows us to get away with relatively large models.
    +   And that's what a lot of signal processing applications look like.

## That's not what all applications look like

```{r}
#| fig-cap: Test scores vs. enrollment in fake Israeli schools
school = read.csv('israel-schools-1200-points.csv')
school = school[school$enrollment < 80, ]
school$enrollment = round(school$enrollment)

ggplot(school) + geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=score), alpha=.2) 
```

Enrollment has some predictive power, but there's a ton of variation.

## To get closer to these applications, let's scale up our errors
-   We can't really do it with the compression errors we've been using.
-   But we can do it with random errors.
-   And often, random errors will give you the same behavior.
-   You can think of random errors as a **model** for your non-random ones.

Here's our compression errors and random ones with matched variance.

:::: {.r-stack}

```{r}
errors = pmap_dfr(list(compressed.curves, curves, sigmas, as.list(names(curves))), function(mu.compressed, mu, sigma, curve) {
    Z = sqrt(3)*runif(10, min=-1, max=1)
    data.frame(X=X,
               compression = mu.compressed(X) - mu(X),
               random      = sigma*Z,
               curve=curve)
})
```


::: {.fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="0"}
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 4
#| layout-valign: bottom
#| fig.width: 3
#| fig.asp: .9
for(curve in names(curves[two.curves])) {
  print(ggplot(errors[errors$curve==curve, ]) + geom_point(aes(x=X, y=compression)))
  print(ggplot(errors[errors$curve==curve, ]) + geom_point(aes(x=X, y=random)))
}
```
Take a look. Guess which is which.
:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible data-fragment-index="0"}
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 4
#| layout-valign: bottom
#| fig.width: 3
#| fig.asp: .9
for(curve in names(curves[two.curves])) {
  print(ggplot(errors[errors$curve==curve, ]) + geom_point(aes(x=X, y=compression), color='red'))
  print(ggplot(errors[errors$curve==curve, ]) + geom_point(aes(x=X, y=random),      color='purple'))
}
```
The red ones are compression errors. Let's fit models with the purple.
:::

::::

## But we're left with an uncomfortable choice

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig.width: 4
#| fig.asp: 1
plot = plots(X, sigmas, formulas, point.alpha=.2)
plot$random('sin',  'twopiece.linear',  noiseless.alpha=0)
plot$random('sin', 'fivepiece.linear', noiseless.alpha=0)
```
-   The smaller models can't always capture the trend.
-   The bigger models exhibit some weird artifacts.


## There's got to be something better than this
-   There is an inevitable trade-off between the flexibility 
    to fit the stuff we want and tendency to fit the stuff we don't.
-   But the knobs we have to fiddle with may not be the ones we want.
-   If we're talking about piecewise-polynomial fits, we've got two knobs.
    +   The degree of each polynomial.
    +   The number of breaks.
-   These don't complement each other very well.

# Let's fiddle with them a little and try to fit some data

## The Data
```{r}

psat = data.frame(x=c(180, 185, 187, 190, 191, 195, 199, 205, 207, 210, 212, 215, 217, 219, 
                      220, 227, 225, 227, 229, 230, 232, 232, 235, 237, 238, 240, 240, 240),
                  y=c(10,    0,   6,  11,   5,   7,  12,   3,   1,   4,  11,   5,   3,  10,
                       9,    11,  13, 6,   15,  21,   6,  12,   2,   9,  0,   0,   0.2,  0.4))
plot.data = data.frame(x=seq(180, 240, .1))
```
```{r}
plot.fit = function(model) { 
  plot.data$y.hat = predict(model, newdata = plot.data)
  ggplot() + geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y.hat), data=plot.data, color='blue') +
             geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y), data=psat)
}

ggplot(psat, aes(x=x,y=y)) + geom_point()
```

## Linear fit 
```{r}
model = lm(y ~ x, data=psat)
plot.fit(model)
```

## Cubic polynomial fit
```{r}
model = lm(y ~ poly(x,3), data=psat)
plot.fit(model)
```

## 5th-order polynomial fit
```{r}
model = lm(y ~ poly(x,5), data=psat)
plot.fit(model)
```

## 7th-order polynomial fit
```{r}
model = lm(y ~ poly(x,7), data=psat)
plot.fit(model)
```

## 9th-order polynomial fit
```{r}
model = lm(y ~ poly(x,9), data=psat)
plot.fit(model)
```

## 11th-order polynomial fit
```{r}
model = lm(y ~ poly(x,11), data=psat)
plot.fit(model)
```

## This just doesn't work

-   Low-order polynomials (e.g. lines, cubics) can't fit the data.
-   High-order polynomials exhibit weird **non-local** behavior.
-   To fit better where there's more data,   
    they'll do crazy things where there isn't much.
-   You might hope that a piecewise polynomial fit would be better.

## A piecewise-cubic fit

```{r}
model = lm(y~poly(x,3) * I(x > 200) * I(x > 220), data=psat)
plot.fit(model)
```

##  This may be even worse.
-   Polynomials can do weird things at the boundaries of the data.
-   Now we've put boundaries in the middle of the data, too.
-   These problems are like the ones from lab, but worse.
    +   In lab, our observations were evenly spaced. That's as good as it gets.
    +   Here, they're not. That's usually the case.
    
##  Fixing this problem is easy.
-   Instead of using all piecewise-polynomial functions, use only ones that:
    +   Are continuous, i.e., with polynomials that match at the breaks.
    +   Are differentiable, i.e., with matched derivatives too.
    +   Maybe twice differentiable, i.e. with matched second derivative too.
-   These functions are called **splines**. 
-   The breaks, where we stitch our polynomials together, are called **knots**.
-   Usually people use cubic polynomials with 
    +   Two matched derivatives
    +   Enough knots to give the flexibility they want.

## These work pretty nicely
```{r}
library(splines)
model = lm(y~bs(x,5), data=psat)
plot.fit(model)
```
A cubic spline with two knots.

## Even with a lot of parameters
```{r}
library(splines)
model = lm(y~bs(x,11), data=psat)
plot.fit(model)
```
A cubic spline with 8 knots.


# Spline Models

##  Splines are linear models.

-   If you add two piecewise-polynomial curves, you get another. 
-   If you add add two differentiable curves, you get another.
-   So if you add two differentiable piecewise-polynomial curves, ...
```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig.width: 4
#| fig.asp: 1
psat2 = psat
psat2$y = sqrt(psat$y)+.9*psat$y
model1 = lm(y~poly(x,3) * I(x > 200) * I(x > 220), data=psat)
model2 = lm(y~poly(x,3) * I(x > 200) * I(x > 220), data=psat2)
y.hat = predict(model1,   newdata=plot.data)
y.hat.2 = predict(model2, newdata=plot.data)
ggplot() + geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y.hat), data=plot.data, color='blue') +
           geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y.hat.2), data=plot.data, color='red') +
           geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y.hat.2+y.hat), data=plot.data, color='purple', linetype=2) 

psat2 = psat
psat2$y = sqrt(psat$y)+.9*psat$y
model1 = lm(y~bs(x,5),    data=psat)
model2 = lm(y~bs(x,11),   data=psat2)
y.hat = predict(model1,   newdata=plot.data)
y.hat.2 = predict(model2, newdata=plot.data)
ggplot() + geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y.hat), data=plot.data, color='blue') +
           geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y.hat.2), data=plot.data, color='red') +
           geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y.hat.2+y.hat), data=plot.data, color='purple', linetype=2) 
```
To use spline models, we'll need a basis. That's easy enough.

## A Basis for Splines with Knots at Zero 
For a cubic spline with one knot at zero, we can work out a general formula.
$$
\begin{align*}
m_{\beta}(x) 
&= \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \beta_3 x^3 \right) \\
&+\left(\beta_{0,+} + \beta_{1,+} x + \beta_{2,+} x^2 + \beta_{3,+}x^3 \right)1(x \ge 0).
\end{align*}
$$
with these continuity and differentiability constraints:

::: {.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="0"}
$$
\begin{align*}
\beta_{0} &= \beta_{0} + \beta_{0,+} && \text{ continuous at zero } \\
\beta_{1} &= \beta_{1} + \beta_{1,+} && \text{ differentiable at zero } \\
\beta_{2} &= \beta_{2} + \beta_{2,+} && \text{ twice-differentiable at zero } \\
\end{align*}
$$
which gives us the simplified form
$$
\begin{align*}
m_{\beta}(x) 
&= \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} x + \beta_{2} x^2 + \beta_{3}x^3 + \beta_{3,+}x^3 1(x \ge 0).
\end{align*}
$$
Generalizing this to splines with knots elsewhere is pretty easy.
:::


## A Basis for Splines 

For a cubic spline with knots at $x_1 \ldots x_k$, there's a similar formula.
$$
\begin{align*}
m_{\beta}(x) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \beta_3 x^3 + \sum_{k=1}^K \beta_{3,k}(x-x_k)^3 1(x \ge x_k).
\end{align*}
$$
This is easy enough to implement plug into `R`, but you won't have to.   
It has splines integrated into its formula language.

## Boundary Issues
Splines like this don't do a great job past the boundary of the data.
```{r}
long.plot.data = data.frame(x=seq(170,240, by=.1))
model = lm(y~bs(x,5),   data=psat)
y.hat = predict(model, newdata=long.plot.data)
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y), psat) + geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y.hat), data=long.plot.data, color='blue')
```
-   Obviously we don't know much about what we should predict there.  
-   But continuing a polynomial that fit in the range of the data leads to counterintuitive predictions.
-   There's no evidence here justifying the steep dive we see on the left.


## Natural Splines
**Natural cubic splines** satisfy an additional constraint.   
They are linear at, and beyond, the edges of the data. 
```{r}
long.plot.data = data.frame(x=seq(170,240, by=.1))
model = lm(y~ns(x,5),   data=psat)
y.hat = predict(model, newdata=long.plot.data)
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y), psat) + geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y.hat), data=long.plot.data, color='blue')
```
-   This is probably what you want. 
-   Finding a basis for these is a bit more complicated.
-   But `R` will do it for you.

## Defaults

-   Natural cubic splines are a good model to use by default.
-   Next week we'll talk about a **local polynomial regression**.
-   If you're doing regression in 1D, you're pretty safe using either. 
-   The week after next we'll talk about higher-dimensional data.
-   That's where model choice gets complicated. 
    +   There aren't really any good universal defaults.
    +   That's where you come in.

# Regression with Transformed Outcomes

## Sometimes the outcome we observe isn't what we want to predict

```{r}
#| fig-ncol: 2 
school = read.csv('israel-schools-1200-points.csv')
school = school[school$enrollment < 80, ]
school$enrollment = round(school$enrollment)

ggplot(school) + geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=score), alpha=.2) 
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=1*I(score >= 1)), alpha=.1, data=school)
```
-   Maybe we're not interested in predicting test scores themselves.
-   We might be interested in predicting whether they exceed a threshold $T$.
-   We can fit a curve that does that.

We do it by predicting an **indicator** that the score exceeds the threshold.
$$ Y_i = 1(\text{score}_i \ge T) $$


## Predicting an indicator
```{r}
model = lm(I(score > 1)~bs(enrollment,5),   data=school)
x = seq(1,80, by=.1)
y.hat = predict(model, newdata=data.frame(enrollment=x))
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=1*I(score >= 1)), alpha=.1, data=school) + 
           geom_line(aes(x=x,y=y.hat), color='blue')
```
We can and often do fit models to indicators via least squares.
$$
\hat \mu = \argmin_{m \in \mathcal{M}} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \{ Y_i - m(X_i) \}^2. 
$$

:::: {.r-stack }

::: {.fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="0"}
-   The curve this estimates is, as usual, essentially the mean of $y$ at a given $x$. 
-   And because $y$ is an indicator, its mean is a **frequency**.
-   It's the proportion of observations at $x$ you expect to exceed the threhold.
:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible data-fragment-index="0"}
-   The main difference is that the plots are hard to look at.
-   The transformed observations all lie on top of each other.
:::

::::

## Sometimes the outcome we observe is hard to predict linearly

This happens, in particular, when there's **exponential growth**.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.asp: .5
#| 
set.seed(1)
x = seq(0,5,by=.2)
y=exp(x + rnorm(length(x))/2)
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y))
```

:::: {.r-stack }

::: {.fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="0"}
-   In financial data, this arises from compound interest.
-   In disease data, this happens because sick people make people sick.
:::

::: {.fragment .current-visible data-fragment-index="0"}
We could try to fit this outcome using a linear model for fast-growing curves.
$$ m_{\beta}(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 e^{x} + \beta_2 e^{2x} + \ldots $$
But it often makes more sense to fit the outcome's logarithm.
$$ Y_i = \log(\text{outcome}_i). $$
:::

::::
## Predicting a log
```{r}
#| fig.ncol: 2
model = lm(log(y)~ns(x,5))
mu.log = predict(model, newdata=data.frame(x=x))
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=log(y))) + geom_line(aes(x=x,y=mu.log), color='blue')
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_line(aes(x=x, y=exp(mu.log)), color='blue')
```
- We fit the logarithm via least squares using a more typical linear model.
- Then we exponentiate its predictions to predict the observed outcome.


$$
\text{outcome at x} \approx e^{\hat \mu_{log}(x)} \ \text{ where } \ \hat\mu_{log} = \argmin_{m \in \mathcal{M}}  \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{ \log(\text{outcome}_i) - m(X_i) \}^2. 
$$

## Other transformations
You can fit other transformations of the outcome you observe.

$$ 
\begin{align*}
\hat \mu(X_i) &\approx Y_i^2 && \text{squares} \\
\hat \mu(X_i) &\approx \sqrt{Y_i} && \text{square roots} \\
\hat \mu(X_i) &\approx f(Y_i) && \text{any function of the outcome at all}
\end{align*}
$$

It's very normal to do this.

-   There's nothing special about the variables you have in your dataset.
-   If you observe some variables, you observe all functions of them, too.
-   In fact, what you observe is often not what was originally collected.
    +   People transform, save, and redistribute data all the time.
    +   What you get reflects the thinking of the person you got the data from.

# Where Errors Come From

## Errors in Signal Processing

![](noisy-pencil-image.jpg)

In signal processing, it's easy to think of where errors come from.

-   Compression, like recoving a signal from an MP3.
-   Energy leakage in digital photography.
-   Quantum fluctuations in low-light photography.

In short, it's physics stuff.  
That's why it's nice to talk about signal processing.

## Errors in Social Science Data


```{r}
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.asp: .7
#| 
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=score), alpha=.2, data=school)
```

In social science data, it's not so easy.

-   There's always going to be variation.
-   No two people, schools, etc. are going to be exactly alike.
-   But usually some of the variation we see can be explained.

## Explaining Variation
```{r}
#| fig.ncol: 2
#| fig.asp:  1
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=score), alpha=.4, data=school[school$msa=='haifa',]) + ylim(0,4)
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=score), alpha=.4, data=school[school$msa=='jerusalem',]) + ylim(0,4)
```

If we break our test scores data down by city, some of the variation goes away.

## Explaining More Variation
```{r}
#| fig.ncol: 2
#| fig.asp:  1
pop.cut.jerusalem = median(school$pop[school$msa=='jerusalem'])
pop.cut.haifa     = median(school$pop[school$msa=='haifa'])
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=score), alpha=.4, color='blue', data=school[school$msa=='haifa' & school$pop <= pop.cut.haifa,]) + 
           geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=score), alpha=.4,  color='red',  data=school[school$msa=='haifa' & school$pop >  pop.cut.haifa,]) + ylim(0,4)
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=score), alpha=.4, color='blue', data=school[school$msa=='jerusalem' & school$pop <= pop.cut.jerusalem,]) + 
           geom_point(aes(x=enrollment, y=score), alpha=.4,  color='red',  data=school[school$msa=='jerusalem' & school$pop >  pop.cut.jerusalem,]) + ylim(0,4)
```

If we break it down by school-district population density too, even more does.

## Explaining it all?

$$ Y_i = \underset{\textcolor{lightgray}{\text{trend}}}{\mu(X_i, \text{etc}_i)}  + \underset{\textcolor{lightgray}{\text{error}}}{\varepsilon_i} $$

-   In this context, what we mean by errors depends on what we model.
-   It's just variation we aren't able to explain.
-   You can imagine that if you had enough info, there'd be no variation left.
    +   Like a clean, uncompressed audio signal
    +   Or a perfectly sharp image
    +   Or whatever that would be for a school  
-   But that's really just an abstraction. 
    +   We won't get there. 
    +   Often we won't get close.
-   That's why it's a pain talking about social science data.
    +   It's hard to describe what you want to explain and what you don't.
    +   We'll develop some language later, but it'll take a while.


## Good news!

-   Until we've got that language, we'll basically stick to signal processing.
-   It may sound like we're talking about social science, but we'll be using fake data.
-   That means we'll know exactly what the **clean signal** is and how it's compressed.
-   Working with well-thought-out fake data is a good way to check your approach.
-   If your approach fails on fake data, why would you trust it on the real stuff?
